routeSelection.basis: The normalized source registration is B Archeologie with teaching language Dutch. The adopted 2026–27 OER formally distinguishes the Dutch-language Archeologie trajectory from English-language Archaeology; the Dutch trajectory and its 12-EC Bachelorscriptie Archeologie are selected.

alternatives.label: Archaeology, art & historical interpretation
alternatives.concept: Studies past societies through actual artefact analysis, world and Greek archaeology, ancient democratic heritage, art, history and literary sources. Geological field mapping, soil analysis and GIS add specific landscape and material-evidence methods. Philosophical and rhetorical texts support interpretation of ancient communities. Modern art and historical research broaden the composition; they do not become ancient archaeology. This is a qualified material-culture response, with substantial gaps in the European period sequence, archaeological excavation, archaeometry and an archaeology thesis.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed composition combines archaeology with substantial art, historical/textual interpretation and environmental methods. The label represents that combination rather than calling all24 courses ancient-society or archaeological study.
progression: All actual offerings/prerequisites pass. Gateway precedes Earth Observation. First-year archaeology/art/literature foundations precede advanced museums, heritage and interpretation. Dynamic Earth in semester3 precedes the semester4 soil/GIS field-method complement. Historical research in American Century is generic historical-method preparation, not an ancient-source project. Six300-level courses and Year1 PPD.

alternatives.label: Cultural heritage, museums & public memory
alternatives.concept: Studies how material culture and cultural memory are interpreted, displayed and contested. Archaeology, Greek democratic heritage, African heritage and restitution, museum/curatorial analysis and art-historical methods form the object-based core. Indigenous public-history work, racial representation, life narratives, qualitative inquiry, decolonial civil-society theory and ethics support specific questions of whose histories institutions tell and how communities participate. Documentary and classical rhetorical practice provide public interpretation tools; these are not archaeological field or heritage-management qualifications.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum concentrates on museums, heritage ethics, public memory, restitution, community interpretation and documentary communication. The label reflects that institutional and public-facing emphasis.
progression: All actual offerings/prerequisites pass, with nine advanced courses and Year1 PPD. Art/archaeology foundations precede advanced heritage and museums; sociology precedes advanced civil-society theory. Primary/public-history, memory narrative and qualitative research support public interpretation with no guaranteed archaeological project subject.
alternatives.distinctness: The programmes share16courses and each has8unique courses/60EC. The first prioritises ancient literary/political interpretation and physical landscape/GIS/data methods; the second replaces that strand with public history, life narratives, sociology/qualitative inquiry/civil-society theory and ethics. This changes the research object and methods used to interpret institutional and community heritage, beyond the numerical floor.

core: Archaeological and material evidence for understanding past societies
Excavation, scientific material analysis and digital archaeological methods
Mediterranean and European societies from prehistory to the early modern period
Archaeological heritage, museums, management and public interpretation
Historical landscapes, cities and human–environment relations
Source criticism, archaeological theory, research and publication
adjacent: Ancient societies through archaeology, history, texts and material culture
Cultural heritage, museums and public memory
Professional field archaeology and archaeometric investigation
questions: What can objects and material remains reveal about past people and societies?
How should archaeological heritage be interpreted, managed and communicated today?
How did people interact with historical landscapes and cities?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Chemical, thermodynamic/mechanical and elementary modelling foundations, with biopolymer preparation/measurement, support the later environmental soil and geospatial investigation of landscape evidence. These are real scientific foundations and laboratory skills, not archaeological materials science.

Studies late-medieval/Renaissance to contemporary Western art, with close painting analysis, on-site artwork study and evidence-based art-historical interpretation. This is a concrete visual-source and museum-context foundation, not ancient artefact or excavation training.
examines the formation and decline of empires, including the political structures within which Mediterranean and European material cultures developed

Actual artefact measurement/cataloguing, technical drawing, craft interpretation, archaeological database/literature research and a contemporary material-evidence project directly implement object-based archaeology. No full excavation sequence is inferred.
directly studies Greek archaeology and reconstructs community and democratic decision-making from material remains
reads major texts from Gilgamesh onward, supplying written cultural evidence that can be interpreted alongside material remains
examines ancient myths and epics across cultures and how they shaped later cultural memory
teaches data cleaning, visualisation and work with spatial data as general digital methods relevant to documenting and analysing evidence, without claiming digital archaeology
treats historical media technologies as material objects whose physical properties shape the circulation and preservation of knowledge

Actual rock/mineral observation, stratigraphy, geological mapping, cross-sections and Ardennes field reporting develop landscape/material field evidence. These are substantial geological methods, not archaeological excavation or finds processing.
provides hands-on GIS, remote-sensing and drone-data analysis relevant to historical landscapes while remaining environmental rather than archaeological field training

Uses soil coring, field/laboratory soil chemistry, microscopy, ICP interpretation and seismic/resistivity/electromagnetic surveys to characterize soils and aquifers. Specific complementary methods for landscape/subsurface evidence, not a substitute for archaeological excavation or dating.
follows warfare, weapons and military organisation from Greek and Roman antiquity onward, adding historical interpretation of material technologies
examines heritage, colonial acquisition, looting and repatriation through African art and museum collections
connects ancient Greek material culture and democratic practice to their contested modern heritage
examines museums, curatorial practice and exhibition strategies as institutions through which material heritage is interpreted

Studies Greek and Roman rhetorical history, original persuasive techniques, argumentation, debates and speeches. These give specific classical-text interpretation and public-explanation practice for the material-culture/heritage concepts; a heritage project is not guaranteed.

Interprets political thought from classical antiquity onward through original texts, historical contexts and comparative argument. It supports interpretation of ancient community, authority and democratic heritage rather than an archaeology theory sequence.
Art-historical historiography from the16thcentury to present and its interpretive methods; not archaeological excavation publication training.

Current Researching the American Century teaches research-question formulation, critical source engagement, methodological rigour and a substantial historical research paper. Provides specific historical-research process skills; neither a Walcheren expedition project nor ancient-source/excavation research is assumed.
combines critical study of documentary form with producing a short documentary for wider audiences
supplies the modern political and social history within which museums, national heritage institutions and public uses of the past developed

Uses Indigenous storywork, historical sources, relational accountability and public-history multimedia collaboration to examine whose histories are represented and how communities participate. A specific public-memory/restitution complement, without claiming European excavation or museum training.

Studies social boundaries, identity, stratification and exclusion through historical sociological theory and an evidence-based social-problem paper. These provide specific frameworks for evaluating institutional representation and community inclusion; a heritage topic is not guaranteed.
teaches qualitative research into meaning, power and public experience, supporting audience and community research in heritage settings

Analyzes memory, identity, trauma, ethics and autobiographical truth in memoir/diary/travel narratives, with an independent life-narrative project. Supports interpretation of remembered lives and public narratives rather than archaeological material analysis.
provides ethical frameworks for questions of ownership, restitution, stewardship and obligations to past and present communities

Studies institutions, public spheres, hegemony, solidarity and decolonial civil-society theory, then researches an organization or movement. This informs institutional authority and community participation in heritage interpretation; a heritage case topic is not guaranteed.

candidates.label: Excavation, archaeological science & field investigation
candidates.assessment: Actual UCR archaeology includes artefact cataloguing/drawing and a small material-evidence project; Dynamic Earth adds stratigraphy and geological field mapping, and Soils & Aquifers adds real coring, geophysical surveys and analytical laboratory methods. These are fully credited. They still do not construct a sustained archaeological excavation/finds-processing/chronometric or archaeometric sequence sufficient to organize another24-course response. This is a substantive disciplinary-construction limit, not missing offering coverage.

selection.assessment: Two qualified related responses remain after programme-level and per-course challenge: material culture with physical landscape/textual methods, and institutional/community heritage with public-memory methods. Shared direct archaeology and ancient-heritage22.5EC sits within substantial art, heritage, historical and material-source study. Each composition now gives concrete roles to all courses. Eightunique courses/60EC each change objects and methods. The separately tested excavation/archaeometry candidate lacks a sustained archaeological field/scientific sequence despite UCR’s real artefact, geological-field and analytical-lab contributions. Stop at two.

notes.text: VU combines sustained European archaeological study with excavation, scientific and digital archaeology, two field schools and a 12 EC individual thesis. UCR offers actual artefact cataloguing and drawing, Greek archaeology and ancient heritage, with related art/history study. The landscape direction adds geological field mapping and soil/geophysical laboratory work; the heritage direction adds public-history and institutional/community interpretation. These are substantive related responses, not full archaeological training.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Archaeology studies past societies through material remains, historical evidence and landscapes. The programme combines Mediterranean and European archaeology with scientific and digital methods, two field schools, critical heritage study and an individual archaeology thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers two qualified related directions: archaeology, art and historical interpretation; and heritage, museums and public memory. World and Greek archaeology and ancient democratic heritage connect with substantial art, material-culture and historical study. The first adds geological field mapping, soil analysis and GIS; the second emphasizes institutions, community histories and memory. Neither reproduces VU’s full European archaeological sequence, excavation training, archaeological materials science or required thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC comprises 138 EC of required courses, a 12 EC thesis including its compulsory colloquium, and 30 EC of free academic choice. Thesis entry requires completion of all first- and second-year courses. Field School 1 requires What is Archaeology; Field School 2 requires Field School 1. Listed practicals require 85% attendance or applicable replacement work. A first-year language test and remediation when needed carry no extra credits. The usual first-year study-advice threshold is 48 EC. Free-choice level, overlap and approval rules apply.

componentNotes.thesis: Required 12 EC individual Dutch-language thesis, including the compulsory colloquium. The English-language thesis is the alternative for the English route, not an additional component.
componentNotes.choice: 30 EC of free academic choice, subject to level, overlap, entry and applicable approval rules.
